newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Britain's Labour increases lead further.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Britain's Labour increases lead further.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party has boosted its strong chances of winning the imminent election after a convincing by-election victory last week, Reuters survey of forecasts by leading experts in election trends showed on Wednesday.

The average of 20 forecasts from a panel of psephologists and pollsters pointed to a 59-seat Labour majority in the new parliament, up from the panel's average prediction in February of a 48-seat majority, and 43 in January.

More than half the panellists questioned on March 3 and 4 said Labour's success in the Wirral South by-election last week had strengthened the likelihood of a resounding majority over the Conservative party, which has been in power since 1979.
Wirral was the main reason Paul Whiteley, Professor of Politics at the University of Sheffield, revised his forecast of Labour's overall majority sharply upwards to 91 seats.

"Wirral has been a big shock. It will encourage people who have traditionally voted Conservative and who have been wavering about Labour now to vote Labour," Whiteley said. "As it's happened so close to the election, the effect should carry on to polling day."
Whiteley, who was unobtainable at the time of the February survey, had previously put Labour's overall majority at 51 seats.

Wirral South, a northern England constituency which traditionally voted Conservative, gave Labour candidate Ben Chapman a 7,888 majority in an 18 percent swing from the Conservatives at the 1992 election.
This has left Prime Minister John Major in a parliamentary minority with 322 seats, one less than all the other parties combined.
All the panellists expect the election to take place on May 1.

"I had expected some signs of a Conservative recovery, but the Wirral by-election put paid to that. There is evidence of direct switching of allegiances in Wirral on a large scale," said Peter Kellner, an independent political analyst, who saw Labour winning 93 more seats than all other parties combined, up from his previous prediction of 77.
Panellists agreed the swing to Labour in Wirral was unlikely to be repeated on the same scale in the election. Eighty-two percent of eligible voters turned out in the 1992 election.

While not all contributors agreed that Wirral had made a massive difference to their predictions of Labour's prospective victory, the by-election result prompted David Carlton of the University of Warwick to drop his previously consistent forecast of a nine-seat victory for the Conservatives.
Carlton now predicted a hung parliament, with no party in overall majority.

The results were in line with the general trends of published opinion polls, many of which are the basis for the political scientists' own forecasts in the panel, giving Labour a 43 percent share of the national vote and the Conservatives 36 percent. The Liberal Democrats would get 16 percent and other parties six percent.

A Reuters/NOP opinion poll of 1,049 voters on February 21 put support for Labour at 50 percent and the Conservatives at 30 percent. A poll this week by ICM for the Guardian newspaper which was conducted after the Wirral vote gave Labour 51 percent and the Conservatives 27 percent, representing a widening of Labour's lead by seven percentage points since ICM's previous poll in February.

Overall, the survey showed Labour expected to win 357 seats of the 659 seats in the new parliament, up from 351 seats predicted in February. The Conservative tally was seen falling to 251 from 257 seats the previous month. The Liberal Democrats were expected to win 25 seats.
Experts said the most important election issues were perceived government incompetence, the economy, education and healthcare.
